posts.title: Thoughts from early in my career
posts.excerpt: Tomorrow marks three months in my first full-time role. I want to keep notes of my thoughts as I move through my career and expect that this will be the first of many notes I write.
paragraphs: Tomorrow marks three months in my first full-time role. I want to keep notes of my thoughts as I move through my career and expect that this will be the first of many notes I write. This first one covers more than just the adjustment to a new job, but my transition from being a student into my career.

First, some perspective. The tech job market (and non-tech too) is tough right now, and I know a lot of hard-working people who are fighting for employment. I am extremely grateful to be both employed and working in a field that I am passionate about and knowledgeable in. Additionally, Morgan Stanley has some very smart people and has overall been a great place to start a career, and I don't take that for granted.

One big adjustment has been the mindset switch around work. This is my first full-time position and work on systems and with a team whose workday does not end at 5 pm everyday. Instead, there is constant communication between people from all over the world regarding systems that run 24/7/365. Coming from working part-time and my academic career, I've had this understanding that work stays at work. This could not be more true working in production. Working outside of the 9-5 schedule is not irregular; neither is working weekends. I feel I had some friction with this idea initially, but seeing the leadership at the company work in this way normalizes it. With the idea in mind that as my career progresses, so will my responsibilities, including being responsible for work outside of the workday, I have an easier time adjusting.

This idea, of course, depends on the ability to work from outside the office, which has been such a blessing. Thus far, I have made a great effort to work in the office as much as possible; when I am in Utah, it is my goal to be in the office every day.

Another adjustment is the pace of progression. Through school, both high school and college, there is a very short (relative) transition from underclassmen to upperclassmen. This is true as well with entry-level work where it is expected that you become proficient in your role within a couple of weeks or months. Three months is not a lot of time, but it is very clear to me that I will be 'new to the role' for likely the next 9 months. I have a general grasp of what my team's responsibilities are and what is expected of me as I progress, but it's clear that becoming an expert in the field takes close to a decade. The volume of information and knowledge that can be learned requires a slow pace of progression.

Despite not being proficient in the work, I really enjoy what our department does. In my personal life, I tend to keep things clean and organized, both physically and digitally. While I enjoy cleaning and organizing, something I enjoy even more is things already being clean and organized. (AI is the ultimate tool for automating organizational tasks, and while I feel like an AI power user, I believe there is significantly more that can be done; but more on that in the future). This idea aligns largely with what the best production engineers do. There is no reason that I or anyone else should have to fix the same problem more than a handful of times. I think root cause analysis of tech systems is the perfect bridge between problem-solving that I love and software engineering that I went to school for.

My perspective on the use of AI has shifted significantly both because of my use of it at work and largely because of its undeniable abilities. During my job search, it felt that presenting as an AI power user meant you were making up for lacking talent of your own. Vibe-coded projects mean nothing because you can't explain the technology behind it, nor did you learn anything from it. Online assessments cannot be completed using AI, so you must study computer science topics yourself. At Morgan Stanley, there is VERY strong encouragement to embrace AI as much as possible. There is also significantly less pressure to know everything. In many cases, it's quicker and simpler to ask AI or Google questions about stuff I probably learned and was tested on in College. Beyond that, my goal is to give as much work to Copilot as possible, as it's my belief that Copilot is smarter than me (maybe not, but at the very least significantly faster than me (and definitely would be smarter than me with the right access and context (more later))). I've put a lot of time into giving Copilot the tools it needs to complete tasks that ordinarily I would do myself. While it's still early, this has been working out; my Copilot workspace is now both faster and smarter than me and writing scripts than I ever expect to be.

While AI use is strongly encouraged, there are many restrictions. Unlike my use of AI in my personal life, Copilot is limited to what it can do and what it can see in a way that reduces its abilities. As of now, Copilot acts more as my personal assistant than it does as a coworker. This means constant check-ins for permissions and asking me to feed it information that it doesn't have access to. It is still efficient, as it can do tedious work that I don't have to (and I don't have to pay it). It's obvious that access to sensitive information and production services is not something that can be given out lightly, but this means Copilot's ability to monitor and understand systems is weak.

The other aspect of AI use at Morgan Stanley is how isolated it feels. This reinstates the personal assistant analogy. I have trained my personal assistant to write scripts for me, and it does well. My boss's personal assistant is extremely good at finding discrepancies in logs. But I cannot talk to his assistant and he cannot talk to mine. Yesterday I took time out of my day to send over the repository my assistant uses and its knowledge base to a colleague so that he could spend some time teaching his assistant how to write correct scripts. Instead, an employee that everyone can talk to seems like the simple fix to this. Maybe an employee for writing scripts and another for searching logs. These employees would have access to the team's repo rather than only their direct. Of course, if these employees become too efficient, what will I do?

To close out, I want to say that I'm very happy about where I am. For so long, a job of this nature has been a goal of mine. I will always have bigger goals, but as of now I feel content with where I am and most importantly, where I'm going.

I'm very excited to announce that I will be starting my career as a Reliability Production Engineer at Morgan Stanley. I'm thankful for the opportunity to work and learn from their team of developers and engineers in Salt Lake City. Thanks to FDM Group for the help and encouragement through the recruitment process and for the training that is to come.

This month, I will be celebrating my graduation ceremony with the SDSU College of Sciences, then packing up and leaving San Diego. Thank you to SDSU for a stellar education and an incredible four years.

Finally, I am extremely grateful for my three years at the Mission Bay Aquatic Center. While I am excited to start my career, I will always miss the long summer days with the Watersports Camp and countless weekends spent teaching sailing.

I'm excited to share that this fall, I graduated from San Diego State University with a bachelor's in Computer Science! I'm now entering the job search, looking for opportunities in the tech industry somewhere along the West Coast.

In my three and a half years at SDSU, I've learned and put into practice a wide range of computer science and tech principles and ideas. I'm grateful to have had many knowledgeable and engaging professors, and a friend group of fellow computer science students. Working, learning, and living with engineers provided a motivating sense of camaraderie and served as a support system for difficult concepts and projects.

In addition to my school work, I have gained significant experience in communications, teamwork, and leadership through my job at the Mission Bay Aquatic Center. This job has shaped me as a person, and I'm very grateful to all of my students and coworkers for the positive impact they've had on me.
My four years in San Diego have helped me build both a community and the skills and experiences needed to begin my career.
